memory_update.text: Restaurants should be mapped as a chain of demand formats, franchise systems, approved-vendor gates, foodservice distribution, beverage/coffee inputs, outsourced manufacturing, packaging, kitchen workflow, digital ordering, delivery, labor, and regulation.

Highest-priority chokepoint candidates are controlled franchise supply chains, approved-vendor gates, first-party ordering/loyalty rails, specialty foodservice distribution, and B2B beverage/coffee solutions.

Low-attention bottleneck value may hide in suppliers that are screened as coffee, ingredients, private-label manufacturing, specialty distribution, packaging, route logistics, or food safety rather than as restaurant companies.
Foodservice consolidation can pressure independent restaurants and create catalysts for procurement diversification, regional distributors, cooperative purchasing, and specialty suppliers.
Restaurant digital-mix expansion and first-party loyalty adoption can reallocate value away from third-party delivery marketplaces and toward brands or software/payment rails that own customer data.

Commodity shocks in coffee, chicken wings, beef, dairy, wheat, packaging, and fuel are recurring catalysts that reveal which restaurant systems and suppliers have contracted sourcing, pass-through protection, and scale procurement advantage.
Need latest primary-source 10-K/10-Q and earnings-call checks for WEST, CHEF, PFGC, FARM, THS, AMNF, DPZ, and WING before promoting any company-specific bottleneck claim beyond Layer 2.
Need to separate direct restaurant revenue from broader foodservice, convenience-store, hospitality, institutional, retail grocery, and CPG exposure for all low-attention supplier candidates.

Need broader public-market mapping for packaging, disposables, food-contact materials, food safety testing, kitchen equipment, refrigeration, POS, labor scheduling, loyalty, and restaurant back-office software.

Need to distinguish real bottlenecks from low-margin competitive scale in distribution and private-label manufacturing by checking customer concentration, route density, switching costs, margins, working capital, leverage, and contract durability.

summary: Layer 2A maps Restaurants as a system of demand formats, franchise operating models, procurement rails, distribution density, menu-component suppliers, beverage/coffee programs, digital ordering, delivery economics, labor/real-estate constraints, and regulatory gates. The likely Serenity-style bottleneck zones are not the most visible public restaurant brands alone; they sit in recurring procurement, approved-vendor status, route-density foodservice distribution, captive or semi-captive supply chains, specialty ingredients, beverage solutions, and first-party digital ordering/loyalty rails. This is an industry-chain and catalyst map only, not a security recommendation.

supply_chain_map.node: Consumer restaurant demand by occasion
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Traffic, ticket size, mix shift, off-premise adoption, premiumization, and convenience demand determine volume for every downstream node. For Serenity mapping, this is the broad demand driver, not the bottleneck itself.

supply_chain_map.node: Restaurant formats: QSR, fast casual, coffee/cafe, full-service, independent restaurants
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Different formats stress different supply-chain nodes: QSR stresses standardization and franchise procurement; coffee/cafe stresses beverage ingredients, equipment, and loyalty; independent FSR stresses distributor dependence and purchasing power.

supply_chain_map.node: Franchise operating systems and brand IP
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Franchisors can scale units without owning most restaurant-level labor and rent risk. The operating system can also control vendor lists, menu specifications, training, pricing architecture, loyalty, and procurement behavior.

supply_chain_map.node: Captive or controlled franchise supply chain
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Domino's is the reference model: a franchisor can capture economics from dough manufacturing, food distribution, and recurring franchisee procurement rather than only from royalties. This node can be a chokepoint where franchisees have limited practical alternatives.

supply_chain_map.node: Approved-vendor and menu-specification gates
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Large chains and franchise systems typically require consistency, food safety, volume reliability, audits, and product specifications. Suppliers that pass these gates may hold durable, low-visibility positions behind menus.

supply_chain_map.node: Broadline foodservice distribution
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Broadline distributors aggregate procurement, warehousing, route delivery, credit, and service frequency. The node matters because restaurants often depend on one or two suppliers for recurring operations, but margins can be low and competition must be checked.

supply_chain_map.node: Specialty foodservice distribution
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Specialty distributors such as premium ingredient suppliers to independent and fine-dining customers can benefit from menu complexity, supplier fragmentation, and route density. The node may be underfollowed because it screens as distribution rather than as restaurant infrastructure.

supply_chain_map.node: Cash-and-carry restaurant procurement
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Independent restaurants may rely on cash-and-carry for a meaningful share of procurement. Consolidation or pricing changes can pressure already thin independent restaurant margins and shift demand toward regional distributors or cooperative purchasing.

supply_chain_map.node: Group purchasing organizations and cooperative purchasing
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: For independents without scale, pooled buying can partially offset distributor concentration and commodity inflation. This is a potential hidden software/services/procurement node, but public-market mapping needs more work.

supply_chain_map.node: Coffee, tea, extracts, flavors, and beverage solutions
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Beverages are recurring, high-frequency, brand-sensitive menu components. B2B coffee and beverage platforms can sit behind restaurants, cafes, convenience stores, travel centers, and foodservice operators, making them second-order restaurant beneficiaries.

supply_chain_map.node: Private-label and outsourced food/beverage manufacturing
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Chains and retailers can outsource roasting, blending, packaging, ready-to-drink, sauces, frozen components, and specialty ingredients. Capacity, quality systems, certifications, and customer integration may matter more than brand visibility.

supply_chain_map.node: Protein procurement and processing: chicken wings, beef, seafood, custom proteins
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Protein volatility can drive franchisee unit economics and menu pricing. Contracted procurement, custom processing, and scale sourcing can become structural advantages, as indicated by Wingstop's move toward contracted wing purchases.

supply_chain_map.node: Commodity-sensitive ingredients: coffee, dairy, wheat, oils, beef, chicken, resin, paperboard, fuel
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Commodity moves affect restaurant margins, supplier working capital, pass-through timing, and distributor gross margins. This node is usually not a durable bottleneck by itself but can create catalysts and stress tests.

supply_chain_map.node: Packaging, disposables, paperboard, resin, and food-contact materials
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Off-premise and delivery-heavy restaurants depend on packaging that meets food safety, branding, cost, and environmental rules. This is a low-attention second-order node requiring broader search.

supply_chain_map.node: Kitchen equipment, refrigeration, automation, smart-kitchen workflows
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Kitchen design and automation can reduce labor minutes, improve throughput, shrink footprint, and support off-premise formats. Wingstop's smart-kitchen discussion suggests operational throughput is a catalyst zone.

supply_chain_map.node: First-party digital ordering, app, loyalty, payments, and customer data
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Digital ordering and loyalty can reduce dependence on delivery marketplaces, improve repeat frequency, and generate customer data. This node is strategic for chains and modern cafe formats, but public-market value capture may be split between restaurant brands, POS vendors, payments, and delivery platforms.

supply_chain_map.node: Third-party delivery marketplaces and commission layer
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Delivery can expand reach but dilute margins through commissions, promotions, and operational complexity. Brands with strong first-party rails may be better positioned than marketplace-dependent operators.

supply_chain_map.node: Restaurant labor, scheduling, training, and compliance software
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Labor is a core restaurant constraint. Scheduling, training, wage compliance, and productivity tools can be hidden chokepoints, especially if wage pressure persists.

supply_chain_map.node: Real estate, drive-thru access, small-format store design, and off-premise footprint
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Store footprint determines build cost, payback, labor model, and throughput. Brands with small boxes or off-premise-heavy formats may expand faster, but real-estate scarcity can still be a bottleneck.

supply_chain_map.node: Food safety, traceability, audits, labeling, and regulated inputs
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Approved suppliers must meet chain audits, food safety controls, traceability, and labeling rules. This can protect incumbents and slow substitution, especially for ingredients, beverage solutions, prepared foods, and packaging.

supply_chain_map.node: Independent restaurant working-capital and credit terms
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Distributors often provide service frequency and implicit credit support. Thin independent restaurant margins make payment terms and procurement flexibility important second-order chokepoints.
